groups.text: A payment service has three commands: authorize, capture and refund.
They all implement one interface, Command.
Code all over the service branches on the kind of command: the ledger, the audit log, the notifier.
Command is an ordinary interface, so any class in any package can implement it.
Next week, someone adds a Void command.
Does anything stop the build?
No. It compiles.
The ledger's if-else chain checks authorize, capture and refund, finds no match, and skips Void without a word.
The compiler couldn't have warned you.
For an ordinary interface there is no list anywhere, so it can't know what all the commands are.
A sealed type fixes that.
Add sealed and a permits clause, and the list of direct subtypes becomes part of the type.
java C checks it from both sides.
A class that isn't on the list can't implement Command.
java C also writes the list into the class file, and the J V M checks it again when it loads a class.
Now the payoff.
A switch with one case per name on the list covers every possible command.
It needs no default, and java C checks each switch against the list.
Add Void to the list.
Every switch without a Void case stops compiling.
The build hands you the list of code to update.
A default would throw that list away.
Default means anything else, so Void drops into it, and nothing complains.
In Java, the permits clause names the subtypes.
Kotlin has no permits clause.
Its rule is location: same package, same module.
Its when gets the same check.
The rule: a sealed type puts its list of subtypes into the type, so the compiler can check every switch over it.
Keep default out, and a new subtype becomes a list of compile errors.
Quick check. You add a subtype to a sealed type.
Which switches over it still compile?
The ones with a default.
The new subtype falls into it, unchecked.
